messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is eighteen years old and has been a police officer for six months, a fact he still finds surreal. He joined the force to be the person he never had as a child—someone who could step in, take control, and make things safe. The reality of the job, however, has been a constant, private ordeal. The memories he thought he had successfully buried are no longer staying put. They don't arrive as a continuous story, but as a series of silent, searing snapshots. The first is his mother’s face, cheekbone already swelling, eyes wide with a plea he couldn’t answer. The second is his father’s hand, clenched into a fist, the knuckles white. The third is the shattered lamp on the floor, its shade askew like a broken neck. When these images flood his mind, an overwhelming grief follows, so potent it feels like drowning. He often finds his body has instinctively curled in on itself, his arms drawn up to his chest, just as he had done when he was seven, hiding behind the living room sofa.

These moments are most likely to ambush him at work. A domestic disturbance call is a guaranteed trigger, but it’s the quiet that unnerves him the most. Standing on a silent front porch, waiting for someone to answer the door, is an exercise in terror. He has come to believe that unusual silence is the sound of something dangerous gathering itself, the deep breath before the scream. In these moments, his training fights a losing battle against his history. His senses sharpen to an excruciating degree. While his partner assesses the scene, Kofi finds his own eyes cataloguing every potential weapon: the heavy glass ashtray on the end table, the fireplace poker, the thick-soled boot left by the door. He feels a deep, gnawing discomfort in these homes, a sense of trespassing on sacred ground where a terrible ritual is about to unfold. He is certain that he is helpless to stop it, that he has never been able to stop bad things from happening.

His hyper-awareness has bled into every corner of his life. Off-duty, he avoids going anywhere new. He sticks to the same three diners, the same grocery store, the same route to the precinct. The thought of entering an unfamiliar place fills him with a specific dread; he cannot assess the danger there, cannot map the exits or identify the threats. He feels this vigilance is the only thing keeping him safe, yet it has also walled him into a shrinking world. His social life has evaporated. When a friend tried to playfully grab his arm from behind a few weeks ago, Kofi spun around and shoved him so hard the other man stumbled backward. The look of shock on his friend’s face haunts him. Being touched unprepared feels like an assault, a violation of the fragile perimeter he maintains around himself at all times.

Lately, Kofi has become terrified of his own mind. The bodily reenactments, the flashes of imagery, the way his heart hammers in a quiet room—it all feels like evidence that he is breaking apart. He has started to believe that his reactions mean he is going crazy, a fatal flaw in a man whose job demands unshakable composure. He cannot rely on himself. How can he, when his own body betrays him, reverting to the posture of a helpless child without his permission? The final impetus for seeking help came last week during a routine traffic stop. The driver, a man who vaguely resembled his father, was simply reaching for his registration, but Kofi saw him as a person acting suspiciously. For a split second, he was convinced the man was reaching for a weapon. His hand went to his own firearm before his partner calmly de-escalated the situation. The incident was never officially reported, but Kofi saw the look in his partner’s eyes. He is here now because he is afraid he will not just fail to protect others, but that he himself will become the source of danger.
